title: Chapter 28
paragraphs: By the time Alexey Alexandrovitch reached the racecourse, Anna was already sitting in the pavilion next to Betsy — the pavilion where all the highest society had gathered. She spotted her husband from a distance. Two men, her husband and her lover, were the two centers of her existence, and without help from her outward senses she felt their nearness. She was aware of her husband approaching from a long way off, and could not help following him through the surging crowd in the middle of which he was moving. She watched his progress toward the pavilion, saw him now answering an ingratiating bow with condescension, now exchanging friendly, casual greetings with his equals, now diligently trying to catch the eye of one of this world's great ones, and taking off his big round hat that squeezed the tops of his ears. All these mannerisms of his she knew, and all of them were hateful to her. "Nothing but ambition, nothing but the wish to get on — that's all there is in his soul," she thought; "as for these lofty ideals, love of culture, religion — they're only so many tools for getting on."

From his glances toward the ladies' pavilion (he was staring straight at her, but did not distinguish his wife in the sea of muslin, ribbons, feathers, parasols and flowers) she saw he was looking for her, but she deliberately avoided noticing him.
"Alexey Alexandrovitch!" Princess Betsy called to him; "I'm sure you don't see your wife: here she is."
He smiled his chilly smile.

"There's so much splendor here that one's eyes are dazzled," he said, and he stepped into the pavilion. He smiled at his wife as a man ought to smile on meeting his wife after just parting from her, and greeted the princess and other acquaintances, giving each one what was their due — that is, jesting with the ladies and dealing out friendly greetings among the men. Below, near the pavilion, was standing an adjutant general of whom Alexey Alexandrovitch had a high opinion, noted for his intelligence and culture. Alexey Alexandrovitch struck up a conversation with him.

There was an interval between races, so nothing got in the way of conversation. The adjutant general expressed his disapproval of racing. Alexey Alexandrovitch replied, defending it. Anna heard his high, measured tones, not missing a word, and every word struck her as false and stabbed her ears with pain.

When the three-mile steeplechase was about to begin, she bent forward and watched, with fixed eyes, Vronsky as he went up to his horse and mounted, while at the same time she heard that loathsome, never-ceasing voice of her husband. She was in an agony of terror for Vronsky, but a still greater agony was the never-ceasing, as it seemed to her, stream of her husband's shrill voice with its familiar intonations.

"I'm a wicked woman, a lost woman," she thought; "but I don't like lying, I can't bear falsehood — while for _him_ (her husband) it's the very breath of life. He knows all about it, he sees everything; what does he care if he can talk so calmly? If he were to kill me, if he were to kill Vronsky, I might respect him. No — all he wants is falsehood and propriety," Anna said to herself, not considering exactly what she wanted from her husband, or how she would have liked to see him behave. She did not understand, either, that Alexey Alexandrovitch's peculiar loquacity that day, so maddening to her, was simply the expression of his inward distress and unease. As a child who has been hurt skips about, throwing all his muscles into motion to drown out the pain, in the same way Alexey Alexandrovitch needed mental exercise to drown out the thoughts of his wife that, in her presence and Vronsky's, with the continual repetition of his name, kept forcing themselves on his attention. And it was as natural for him to talk well and cleverly as it is natural for a child to skip about. He was saying:

"Danger in the races of officers, of cavalrymen, is an essential element of the race. If England can point to the most brilliant feats of cavalry in military history, it is simply because she has historically developed this force, both in beasts and in men. Sport, in my opinion, has great value, and as always we see only what is most superficial."
"It's not superficial," said Princess Tverskaya. "One of the officers, they say, has broken two ribs."
Alexey Alexandrovitch smiled his smile, which uncovered his teeth and revealed nothing more.

"We'll grant, princess, that that's not superficial," he said, "but internal. But that's not the point," and he turned again to the general with whom he had been speaking seriously; "we mustn't forget that those taking part in the race are military men, who have chosen that career, and one must admit that every calling has its disagreeable side. It forms an integral part of an officer's duties. Low sports, such as prize-fighting or Spanish bullfights, are a sign of barbarity. But specialized trials of skill are a sign of development."
"No, I won't come another time; it's too upsetting," said Princess Betsy. "Isn't it, Anna?"
"It is upsetting — but one can't tear oneself away," said another lady. "If I'd been a Roman woman I should never have missed a single circus."
Anna said nothing, and, keeping her opera-glass raised, gazed always at the same spot.
Just then a tall general passed through the pavilion. Cutting off what he was in the middle of saying, Alexey Alexandrovitch rose quickly — though still with dignity — and made a low bow to him.
"You're not racing?" the officer asked, teasing him.
"My race is a harder one," Alexey Alexandrovitch answered deferentially.
And though the reply meant nothing, the general looked as if he had heard a witty remark from a witty man, and thoroughly relished _la pointe de la sauce_.

"There are two aspects," Alexey Alexandrovitch resumed: "those who take part and those who watch; and love for such spectacles is an unmistakable proof of a low degree of development in the spectator, I admit, but...."
"Princess, bets!" came Stepan Arkadyevitch's voice from below, calling up to Betsy. "Who's your favorite?"
"Anna and I are for Kuzovlev," Betsy answered.
"I'm for Vronsky. A pair of gloves?"
"Done!"
"But it is a pretty sight, isn't it?"
Alexey Alexandrovitch paused while there was talk going on around him, but he started up again at once.
"I admit that manly sports do not...." he was continuing.

But at that moment the racers started, and all conversation broke off. Alexey Alexandrovitch fell silent too, and everyone stood up and turned toward the stream. Alexey Alexandrovitch had no interest in the race, and so he did not watch the racers, but began listlessly to scan the spectators with his weary eyes. His gaze rested on Anna.

Her face was white and set. She was clearly seeing nothing and no one but one man. Her hand had clutched her fan convulsively, and she was holding her breath. He looked at her and hastily turned away, scanning other faces.

"Well, here's this lady too, and others equally moved; it's perfectly natural," Alexey Alexandrovitch told himself. He tried not to look at her, but unconsciously his eyes were drawn back to her. He examined that face again, trying not to read what was so plainly written on it, and against his own will, with horror, read on it what he did not want to know.

The first fall — Kuzovlev's, at the stream — agitated everyone, but Alexey Alexandrovitch saw distinctly on Anna's pale, triumphant face that the man she was watching had not fallen. When, after Mahotin and Vronsky had cleared the worst barrier, the next officer was thrown straight onto his head at it and fatally injured, and a shudder of horror ran through the whole crowd, Alexey Alexandrovitch saw that Anna did not even notice it, and had some trouble making out what they were talking about around her. But more and more often, and with increasing persistence, he watched her. Anna, wholly absorbed in the race as she was, became aware of her husband's cold eyes fixed on her from one side.
She glanced round for an instant, looked at him questioningly, and, with a slight frown, turned away again.
"Ah, I don't care!" she seemed to be saying to him, and she did not look at him again once.

The race was an unlucky one, and of the seventeen officers who rode in it more than half were thrown and hurt. By the end everyone was in a state of agitation, which was made all the worse by the fact that the Tsar was displeased.
